views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should signal willingness to negotiate while maintaining current retaliatory posture. Do not escalate further — the $200B List 3 is already proposed and additional provocation would trigger it. Use the yuan's 7% depreciation since mid-April as a quiet offset to tariff damage. Engage diplomatically through multiple channels to de-escalate before the situation reaches $500B coverage.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.5 reflects that US tariffs have moved from rhetoric to reality — $34B List 1 is in force (July 6), List 3 ($200B) is proposed (July 10), and Trump has threatened all $500B of Chinese exports. The ZTE denial order (April 16) demonstrated devastating non-tariff leverage: a single Commerce Department action nearly shut down a major Chinese firm, exposing China's dependence on US semiconductor supply chains. China's yuan has depreciated ~7% against the dollar since mid-April, which partially offsets tariff costs but raises capital flight risks reminiscent of the destabilizing 2015 devaluation. J.P. Morgan analysts (July 18) warned the trade war hit during China's critical deleveraging phase, creating a policy bind between tightening for financial stability and loosening for growth. China's retaliatory tariffs on US agriculture (soybeans, pork) target politically sensitive US regions, providing leverage, but China cannot match tariffs dollar-for-dollar given the trade asymmetry ($500B exports vs. $130B imports). The action_score of -0.15 (negotiate) reflects that China has already retaliated in kind and further escalation risks triggering List 3 before its economic damage can be absorbed. The smarter play is to let the yuan depreciation work quietly, engage diplomatically, and avoid giving the US justification for the $200B escalation while the domestic economy absorbs the initial shock.
key_factors: US List 1 ($34B) tariffs in force since July 6 with matching Chinese retaliation
US List 3 ($200B) proposed July 10 — imminent threat of further escalation
ZTE denial order (April) demonstrated devastating non-tariff tech leverage
Yuan depreciated ~7% vs dollar since mid-April — partial offset but capital flight risk
Trade asymmetry limits China's ability to match tariffs dollar-for-dollar
Trade war hit during critical deleveraging phase — policy bind between tightening and growth support
China's agricultural retaliation targets US politically sensitive regions but has limits

sources_cited.excerpt: US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines).
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.

J.P. Morgan: 'The trade war is complicating China's efforts to fix its economy... the timing couldn't have been worse. After years of handwringing, China finally began to focus in earnest on curbing credit growth — its Achilles's heel — from around mid-2017.'

China's currency fell to a near 11-month low. Since June 14, it has lost about 4 percent. Strategists said China has not intentionally driven down the yuan, but it is not taking actions it often takes to stabilize it.
The value of China's renminbi has fallen over 7 percent against the dollar since mid-April. A lower renminbi makes China's exports cheaper to foreign buyers.
